title: The 'Happiness Crash': As Young Adult Happiness Drops, Two Groups Are Thriving https://ifstudies.org/blog/the-happiness-crash-as-young-adult-happiness-drops-two-groups-are-thriving
author: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
source: Institute for Family Studies (ifstudies.org), reprinted from Deseret News, October 2, 2026
summary: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer open with Harry Harlow's isolated monkeys and the research of Cacioppo and Holt-Lunstad to establish that social contact is a biological need. They argue that smartphones, social media, gaming, pornography and chatbots have crowded out face-to-face life for young adults, whose reported unhappiness has more than doubled since 2000. Drawing on a new IFS report, The Devout Difference, they show that married and religious young adults have largely escaped this crash, with 50 percent very happy versus 16 percent of unmarried secular peers. They note the data are not causal but argue that marriage and faith remain the strongest bulwarks against loneliness. The authors then warn that isolated, purposeless young people are vulnerable to radical online movements, citing Eric Hoffer, and hope signs of renewal among Gen Z prove real.
points: Social connection is presented as a biological necessity, so the digital substitution of scrolling for socializing has real health costs.
Weekly socializing among young adults has fallen by more than half, from 12 hours to 5, while social media use averages three hours a day.
Fifty percent of married, religious Americans aged 20 to 35 are very happy compared with 16 percent of unmarried secular peers, and only 7 percent of the former are not too happy.
Marriage rates among those under 35 have fallen from 58 percent to 30 percent since the 1970s, as the share never attending services has risen from 17 to 39 percent.
Isolation breeds vulnerability to radical movements on left and right, so marriage and faith are framed as civic as well as personal goods.
quotes: The results of being isolated for months were devastating: The monkeys rocked, harmed themselves and stared blankly.
Smartphones and social media—not to mention gaming, pornography and AI chatbots—have crowded out face-to-face conversation, socializing, and community life among teens and young adults.
Socializing among young men and women is down more than 50%, from 12 hours to 5 hours per week.

According to the General Social Survey, 50% of married, religious Americans aged 20 to 35 describe themselves as “very happy,” compared with just 16% of their unmarried, secular peers—a threefold difference.
In an age marked by too many screens and too much solitude, faith and family remain two of the strongest bulwarks against loneliness and despair.
In the 1970s, 58% of Americans aged 20 to 35 were married; today, just 30% are.
Marriage and faith answer that craving twice over: They call us to sacrifice for something beyond ourselves, and they bind us to the people we need to survive and thrive.
